children: Gold futures fell sharply Wednesday as the U.S. dollar strengthened and Treasury yields rose to multiyear highs, with Federal Reserve policymakers reaffirming support for last week’s rate hike and warning of inflation risks.
The benchmark 10-year yield, which has a broad impact on borrowing costs across the economy, rose as high as 5.14% on Wednesday—an intraday level not seen since July 2007—before settling at 5.11%.
The two-year note, which is more sensitive to expected Fed interest rate moves, rose to 4.94%, the highest since June 2024, and the 30-year yield hit 5.37%, the highest in 22 years.

"Markets are sending a message to Secretary [Scott] Bessent that his plan to suppress yields is not likely to work," Spartan Capital chief market economist Peter Cardillo said in a note, referring to the Treasury Department's efforts to cool down long-term yields by increasing its buying of long-term bonds, as well as concerns about the expanding U.S. fiscal deficit.

Fed officials have struck a ​hawkish tone this week, with Fed Bank of Chicago President Austan Goolsbee saying the central ​bank may need to treat the current energy shock as a source of persistent inflation rather than ‌expect ⁠it to fade on its own.
The comments follow those of other Fed officials who have broadened their concerns about inflation.
Traders ⁠now see a 77% chance of a rate hike in October and a 95% chance of an increase in December, according to CME's FedWatch ​Tool.

"Post-FOMC Fed ​speak has been fairly hawkish. So the market is building in expectations of at least one ​more rate hike before the end of the year. And that's putting gold under pressure," Zaner Metals senior metals strategist Peter Grant said in a note.
